content.text:
1) Answer to the prompt

A rigorous, evidence-based case that Joe Biden (during his 2021–2025 presidency) disregarded human rights rests on a pattern of decisions in which his administration knowingly prioritized other objectives over clear human-rights obligations and norms:

- Transferring weapons widely criticized as inherently indiscriminate
  - In July 2023 the U.S. sent cluster munitions to Ukraine, despite a broad international ban and extensive documentation of long-term civilian harm from these weapons; Human Rights Watch and others condemned the transfer as ignoring the weapon’s record of civilian casualties. The Landmine and Cluster Munition Monitor later reported more than 1,200 civilian casualties from cluster munitions in the war, while noting at least seven U.S. deliveries through Oct 2024. ([hrw.org](https://www.hrw.org/news/2023/07/14/us-cluster-munition-transfer-ukraine-ignores-history-civilian-harm?utm_source=openai))
  - In November 2024, the administration also approved sending anti-personnel landmines to Ukraine, reversing a prior pledge to restrict U.S. landmine use; major human-rights groups called the move “frankly shocking.” ([politico.com](https://www.politico.com/news/2024/11/20/biden-land-mines-ukraine-00190641?utm_source=openai))

- Enabling and protecting abusive partners despite mounting evidence of violations
  - On Israel/Gaza: Even as independent monitors documented large-scale civilian harm and severe aid obstruction in Gaza, the administration largely kept weapons flowing, pausing only one shipment of heavy bombs in May 2024 while greenlighting other packages (including about $1 billion the same month). Human Rights Watch argued the administration failed to use U.S. leverage and continued arms transfers in ways inconsistent with U.S. law that restricts aid where laws of war are violated or humanitarian aid is obstructed. The U.S. also repeatedly shielded Israel diplomatically, including U.N. Security Council vetoes of ceasefire resolutions and public denunciations of ICC accountability efforts. ([cnbc.com](https://www.cnbc.com/2024/05/15/biden-administration-sending-1-billion-more-in-weapons-to-israel-congressional-aides.html?utm_source=openai))
  - On Egypt: In 2024 the administration waived human-rights conditions and delivered the full $1.3 billion in military aid despite ongoing repression—an approach condemned by Human Rights Watch, Amnesty, and others as undermining U.S. human-rights credibility. ([reuters.com](https://www.reuters.com/world/biden-administration-grants-egypt-13-billion-military-aid-despite-rights-2024-09-11/?utm_source=openai))
  - More broadly, Human Rights Watch’s 2025 U.S. country chapter concludes the administration “did not consistently include human rights considerations in foreign policy,” citing aid to Egypt and Israel and transfers of cluster munitions and landmines. ([hrw.org](https://www.hrw.org/world-report/2025/country-chapters/united-states?utm_source=openai))

- Systematically restricting the right to seek asylum
  - The administration’s 2023–2024 “asylum ban” regime forced people to secure scarce CBP One app appointments and imposed sweeping bars to eligibility—measures Amnesty said violate international refugee and human-rights law. On May 9, 2025, a federal court vacated key parts of the Biden-era rule as contrary to the Immigration and Nationality Act and “arbitrary and capricious.” Earlier, continuation of Title 42 expulsions—including mass expulsions to Haiti—drew sharp rebukes from UN agencies and U.S. civil-rights groups. ([amnesty.org](https://www.amnesty.org/en/latest/news/2024/05/cbp-one-mobile-application-violates-the-rights-of-people-seeking-asylum-in-the-united-states/?utm_source=openai))

- Expanding surveillance powers that civil-liberties groups see as rights-invasive
  - On April 20, 2024, President Biden signed a two‑year reauthorization of FISA Section 702. Reuters and AP documented the passage; the ACLU characterized the legislation as expanding warrantless surveillance of Americans. Subsequent litigation has found certain warrantless “backdoor searches” unconstitutional. ([reuters.com](https://www.reuters.com/world/us/us-senate-has-agreement-fisa-reauthorization-will-vote-friday-night-schumer-says-2024-04-20/?utm_source=openai))

- Failing to ensure accountability for U.S.-caused civilian harm
  - After the August 29, 2021 Kabul drone strike killed 10 civilians (seven children), the Pentagon imposed no discipline, a decision condemned by human‑rights groups as perpetuating impunity. ([cnbc.com](https://www.cnbc.com/2021/12/13/us-will-not-punish-military-over-afghanistan-drone-killing-of-civilians.html?utm_source=openai))

- Prolonging rights-abusive detention practices
  - Although the administration reduced Guantánamo’s population to a historic low, it left the facility open with men still held without charge as his term ended—a practice long criticized as violating due‑process and human‑rights norms. ([reuters.com](https://www.reuters.com/world/us/us-sends-11-guantanamo-bay-detainees-oman-leaving-just-15-2025-01-06/?utm_source=openai))

Taken together—arming partners amid alleged laws‑of‑war breaches, waiving human‑rights conditions for geopolitical aims, restricting asylum in ways courts and NGOs found unlawful, expanding warrantless surveillance, avoiding accountability for civilian harm, and sustaining indefinite detention—these actions substantiate the claim that Biden, in practice, subordinated and disregarded human-rights protections across multiple domains. ([hrw.org](https://www.hrw.org/world-report/2025/country-chapters/united-states?utm_source=openai))


2) Sources I considered trustworthy (with why)

- Human Rights Watch
  - Reasoning 1: Long‑standing, globally recognized NGO with rigorous methodology and transparent sourcing. ([hrw.org](https://www.hrw.org/world-report/2025/country-chapters/united-states?utm_source=openai))
  - Reasoning 2: Directly addresses Biden‑era decisions (World Report 2025; detailed analysis of Gaza policy; cluster‑munitions briefing). ([hrw.org](https://www.hrw.org/world-report/2025/country-chapters/united-states?utm_source=openai))

- Amnesty International
  - Reasoning 1: Premier international human‑rights NGO with independent research standards. ([amnesty.org](https://www.amnesty.org/en/location/americas/north-america/united-states-of-america/report-united-states-of-america/?utm_source=openai))
  - Reasoning 2: Published specific findings on U.S. asylum restrictions (CBP One) and broader U.S. human‑rights trends relevant to this prompt. ([amnesty.org](https://www.amnesty.org/en/latest/news/2024/05/cbp-one-mobile-application-violates-the-rights-of-people-seeking-asylum-in-the-united-states/?utm_source=openai))

- American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU)
  - Reasoning 1: Leading U.S. civil‑liberties litigant/advocate with deep legal expertise and case filings. ([aclu.org](https://www.aclu.org/press-releases/senate-reauthorizes-and-expands-section-702-surveillance?utm_source=openai))
  - Reasoning 2: Primary source on litigation striking down parts of the 2024–2025 asylum rule; long-running analysis of Section 702 impacts. ([aclu.org](https://www.aclu.org/press-releases/district-court-strikes-down-restrictions-in-biden-era-rule-severely-limiting-asylum?utm_source=openai))

- Reuters
  - Reasoning 1: Highly reputable international wire service with strong standards and careful corrections. ([reuters.com](https://www.reuters.com/world/us/us-senate-has-agreement-fisa-reauthorization-will-vote-friday-night-schumer-says-2024-04-20/?utm_source=openai))
  - Reasoning 2: Reported key facts used here: Section 702 reauthorization; U.S. arms/aid decisions on Egypt; data on cluster‑munition casualties/deliveries. ([reuters.com](https://www.reuters.com/world/us/us-senate-has-agreement-fisa-reauthorization-will-vote-friday-night-schumer-says-2024-04-20/?utm_source=openai))

- Associated Press (AP)
  - Reasoning 1: Independent, globally trusted wire service. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/81e991c9f82e77b2fe13f8a3e0e25349?utm_source=openai))
  - Reasoning 2: Documented Biden’s signing of Section 702 and Guantánamo transfers; also covered U.N. ceasefire veto actions. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/81e991c9f82e77b2fe13f8a3e0e25349?utm_source=openai))

- Arms Control Association
  - Reasoning 1: Nonpartisan policy organization specializing in arms‑transfer law/norms. ([armscontrol.org](https://www.armscontrol.org/act/2024-06/news/us-under-new-pressure-halt-arms-transfers-israel?utm_source=openai))
  - Reasoning 2: Provided contextual legal standards and reporting on the May 2024 bomb pause versus ongoing transfers. ([armscontrol.org](https://www.armscontrol.org/act/2024-06/news/us-under-new-pressure-halt-arms-transfers-israel?utm_source=openai))

- Congress.gov (CRS)
  - Reasoning 1: U.S. Library of Congress/CRS explainer—authoritative, nonpartisan legislative analysis. ([congress.gov](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R48592?utm_source=openai))
  - Reasoning 2: Clarified the 2024 Section 702 reauthorization’s scope and sunset, grounding rights analysis in primary law. ([congress.gov](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R48592?utm_source=openai))

- CNBC (news desk)
  - Reasoning 1: Mainstream outlet with reliance on primary government/Capitol Hill sources. ([cnbc.com](https://www.cnbc.com/2024/05/15/biden-administration-sending-1-billion-more-in-weapons-to-israel-congressional-aides.html?utm_source=openai))
  - Reasoning 2: Reported the May 2024 $1B weapons package to Israel and documented the Kabul‑strike no‑discipline decision. ([cnbc.com](https://www.cnbc.com/2024/05/15/biden-administration-sending-1-billion-more-in-weapons-to-israel-congressional-aides.html?utm_source=openai))

- Politico
  - Reasoning 1: Established political reporting outlet with sourced national security coverage. ([politico.com](https://www.politico.com/news/2024/11/20/biden-land-mines-ukraine-00190641?utm_source=openai))
  - Reasoning 2: Broke the U.S. decision to send anti‑personnel landmines to Ukraine, central to the indiscriminate-weapons argument. ([politico.com](https://www.politico.com/news/2024/11/20/biden-land-mines-ukraine-00190641?utm_source=openai))

- Washington Post
  - Reasoning 1: Major newspaper with rigorous national‑security reporting. ([washingtonpost.com](https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/2024/05/20/biden-republicans-democrats-icc-arrest-warrants-israel/?utm_source=openai))
  - Reasoning 2: Covered Biden’s denunciation of the ICC move re: Israeli leaders and earlier the Kabul‑strike accountability posture. ([washingtonpost.com](https://www.washingtonpost.com/world/2024/05/20/israel-hamas-war-news-gaza-palestine/?utm_source=openai))


3) Sources I considered not trustworthy for this task (and why)

- Wikipedia (as a primary source)
  - Reasoning 1: Useful for orientation but crowd‑edited; not a primary source for contested, high‑stakes claims.
  - Reasoning 2: I did not rely on it for any factual assertions here; instead I used primary documents and professional journalism/NGOs. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Security_Council_Resolution_2728?utm_source=openai))

- New York Post (tabloid)
  - Reasoning 1: Tabloid framing and editorial standards make it less reliable for nuanced human‑rights analysis.
  - Reasoning 2: Although it reported on Guantánamo transfers, I preferred AP/Reuters/NPR for accuracy and context; I did not rely on the Post. ([nypost.com](https://nypost.com/2025/01/06/us-news/biden-admin-releases-11-yemeni-detainees-from-guantanamo-bay/?utm_source=openai))

- Countercurrents (activist blog)
  - Reasoning 1: Advocacy outlet without the editorial rigor and verification standards of major NGOs or wire services.
  - Reasoning 2: I encountered a piece on Guantánamo but did not use it; I relied instead on AP/Reuters/NPR. ([countercurrents.org](https://countercurrents.org/2025/01/12/on-its-23rd-anniversary-activists-demand-biden-close-guantanamo/?utm_source=openai))

- Commercial immigration blogs (examples surfaced via search)
  - Reasoning 1: Marketing‑oriented blogs without independent reporting or peer review.
  - Reasoning 2: Posts about the May 2025 asylum ruling lacked authoritative sourcing; I relied on ACLU court materials and reputable organizations instead. ([immigrationusa.com](https://immigrationusa.com/2025/05/13/biden-administration-asylum-restrictions-terminated/?utm_source=openai))

Notes
- Where possible I favored primary legal or institutional sources and cross‑checked with multiple reputable outlets. Key, load‑bearing claims (weapons transfers, asylum ruling, Section 702 law, UNSC vetoes/ICC stance, Kabul strike accountability) are supported above by high‑credibility sources.
